item.title: Jscrambler npm Backdoor, CrashStealer macOS Malware, Nihon Kotsu Outage, First VPN Sanctions
CrashStealer macOS Malware, ModHeader Removal, and Joomla RCE Exploitation Drive Digest
Forg365 Microsoft 365 Phishing, Russian Coms Charges, and EU GRU Sanctions
Russian FSB Router Targeting, Evilginx Microsoft 365 Phishing, and Claude Mythos Vulnerability Research
Jscrambler npm backdoor, CrashStealer, Joomla CVE-2026-48939/56291 exploitation, Russian router threats
item.content:encoded:
iCagenda and Balbooa Forms Joomla Flaws Reportedly Exploited as Zero-Days — Must Read

CISA added critical Joomla extension flaws in iCagenda and Balbooa Forms to its KEV catalog after reports of active zero-day exploitation allowing unauthenticated file uploads and remote code execution. Site owners should urgently update to patched versions and check upload folders for PHP web shells or other signs of compromise.

  • CISA added two maximum-severity Joomla extension vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-48939 in iCagenda and CVE-2026-56291 in Balbooa Forms, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after reports of zero-day exploitation.
  • CVE-2026-48939 allows arbitrary file uploads through iCagenda's file attachment feature, leading to PHP code upload and execution, and affects iCagenda 4.x through 4.0.7 and legacy 3.x versions 3.2.1 through 3.9.14.
  • JoomliC released fixes for CVE-2026-48939 in iCagenda versions 4.0.8 and 3.9.15, and site owners were advised to check the images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/ folder for suspicious PHP files.
  • CVE-2026-56291 affects Balbooa Forms versions up to and including 2.4.0, allows arbitrary file uploads leading to remote code execution, and was patched in version 2.4.1.
  • The Australian Cyber Security Centre warned of a global campaign in which malicious actors are scanning websites to deploy web shells by exploiting vulnerabilities in CMS software and plugins.

US and allies warn of Russian critical infrastructure attacks — Must Read

The U.S. and allies warned that Russian FSB-linked hackers are targeting poorly secured routers, especially those using weak SNMP settings or vulnerable Cisco Smart Install features, to infiltrate critical infrastructure networks. Agencies urged organizations to harden routers by upgrading SNMP, disabling risky services, blocking SNMP/TFTP traffic, patching firmware, and replacing end-of-life devices.

  • Cybersecurity agencies from the United States and eight other countries issued a joint warning that Russian state hackers are targeting vulnerable and poorly configured routers to infiltrate critical infrastructure networks.
  • The joint advisory attributes the activity to hackers from the Russian Federal Security Service Center 16, also tracked as Berserk Bear, Energetic Bear, Crouching Yeti, Dragonfly, Ghost Blizzard, and Static Tundra.
  • The hackers scan internet-connected IP ranges for routers using default or common SNMP authentication strings, then use spoofed IP addresses to copy device configuration files and exfiltrate them via Trivial File Transfer Protocol to actor-controlled servers.
  • The FBI previously warned in August 2025 that the same group had been targeting critical infrastructure since November 2021 by exploiting CVE-2018-0171 in the Smart Install feature of Cisco IOS and Cisco IOS XE software.
  • The advisory urges defenders to upgrade to SNMPv3, disable Cisco Smart Install, enforce strong unique passwords, block TFTP and SNMP traffic at edge firewalls, update software and firmware, and replace end-of-life devices.

Misconfigured Server Reveals Three Evilginx Phishing Operations Targeting Microsoft 365 — Should Read

A misconfigured phishing server exposed three Evilginx-based Microsoft 365 phishing operations that steal or refresh tokens to keep access even after MFA. The key defense is that passkeys/FIDO2 help against reverse-proxy phishing, but device-code phishing requires blocking or tightly restricting Microsoft’s device code flow with Conditional Access.

  • Lexfo found a misconfigured Python web server with directory listing enabled, exposing phishing configurations, credential-harvesting logs, RMM installers, combolists, backup archives, and Telegram session files tied to a Microsoft 365 phishing operation.
  • The exposed server led researchers to three phishing operations using custom forks of the open-source Evilginx proxy, including campaigns linked in the article to codemado, mail-argenta, and saroula01.
  • The operations used two different approaches against Microsoft 365 accounts: Evilginx adversary-in-the-middle proxying of live logins and abuse of Microsoft’s legitimate OAuth device code flow.
  • The black-queen device-code campaign attributed to saroula01 logged 218 distinct captured accounts across a dozen countries between June 2025 and July 2026, with about 94 percent identified as corporate mailboxes.
  • The article says phishing-resistant MFA such as FIDO2 or passkeys can stop Evilginx-style reverse-proxy phishing, but device-code phishing requires Conditional Access controls such as blocking device code flow where possible.

Forg365 PhaaS Targets Microsoft 365 with Device Code and AitM Session Theft — Should Read

Forg365 is a new phishing-as-a-service platform targeting Microsoft 365 that combines device code phishing, adversary-in-the-middle session theft, anti-bot evasion, AI-generated lures, and tools for maintaining access to compromised mailboxes. The key defense is to restrict device code authentication, audit mailbox activity and mail-flow rules, and remove legacy aliases that attackers can abuse for phishing delivery.

  • Forg365 is a phishing-as-a-service operation sold via Telegram for $400 per month or $3,800 per year that targets Microsoft 365 accounts.
  • Forg365 attack chains use phishing lures delivered through legitimate email infrastructure such as Amazon SES and Twilio SendGrid before redirecting victims to Forg365-controlled domains.
  • The platform includes device code phishing that shows a Microsoft-styled verification code page and pushes victims into a legitimate Microsoft Authentication Broker sign-in flow that authorizes an attacker-controlled session.
  • Forg365 provides an operator panel at logfriend[.]com/login for generating lures, setting up campaigns, and managing captured tokens.
  • Forg365 includes a Chromium browser extension called ForgCookie that is designed to maintain access to compromised Microsoft accounts by refreshing and injecting Microsoft session cookies.

EU sanctions Russian GRU military hackers over cyberattacks — Should Read

The EU and UK sanctioned Russian GRU, FSB-linked hackers, cybercriminals, and supporting entities accused of coordinating cyberattacks and influence operations across Europe. Officials tied Russia’s cyber ecosystem to attacks on government networks, critical infrastructure, and Poland’s energy sector.

  • The European Union sanctioned nine individuals and four entities, including Russian GRU officers and cybercriminals, while the United Kingdom separately sanctioned 24 individuals and entities tied to Russian cyber and hybrid operations.
  • The United Kingdom sanctioned senior GRU figures Vyacheslav Stafeyev, Ivan Senin, and Ivan Kasyanenko, members of the IMPULS company, people tied to the Lumma Stealer malware operation, and ten people connected to Rybar LLC.
  • The Council of the European Union publicly identified the 16th Centre of Russia's Federal Security Service as controlling several cyber threat groups, including Turla.
  • Officials said Russia-linked groups targeted government networks and critical infrastructure in multiple European countries and linked Turla to a failed strike against Poland's critical infrastructure that could have cut power to roughly 500,000 people during winter.
  • A late-December cyberattack on Poland's power grid damaged key operational technology equipment beyond repair but failed to disrupt power, and was later attributed to the Russian state-backed hacking group Sandworm.

Hackers backdoor Jscrambler npm package with infostealer malware — Should Read

Jscrambler disclosed that attackers used compromised npm publishing credentials to release malicious versions of its package containing infostealer malware, resulting in about 1,500 downloads before removal. Developers who installed the affected versions should treat their environments as compromised, rotate secrets, and update to the latest safe release.

  • Jscrambler disclosed that a threat actor published malicious versions of its jscrambler npm package used with the company’s Code Integrity product.
  • The malicious releases, versions 8.14, 8.16, 8.17, and 8.20, included information-stealing malware that executed during the preinstall hook.
  • The malicious package remained available for about two hours, was downloaded 1,479 times, and was replaced by safe version 8.22.
  • Socket reported that the malware targeted source code, developer secrets, cloud credentials, AI coding tool configurations, cryptocurrency wallets, browser data, and messaging app data.
  • Jscrambler said the incident was caused by compromised npm publishing credentials, which it revoked, and advised affected developers to treat environments as compromised and rotate all secrets.

CrashStealer macOS Malware Uses Notarized Dropper to Pass Gatekeeper Checks — Should Read

Researchers found CrashStealer, a new native C++ macOS infostealer delivered through a signed and Apple-notarized dropper that can pass Gatekeeper checks. It steals browser credentials, crypto wallet data, password manager data, files, and keychain material before encrypting and exfiltrating it to attacker infrastructure.

  • CrashStealer is a new macOS information stealer implemented in native C++ and analyzed by Jamf Threat Labs.
  • CrashStealer is distributed through a signed and Apple-notarized dropper named Werkbit.app, allowing it to pass Gatekeeper checks because the disk image and binary are notarized and use a valid developer ID.
  • The dropper contacts a GitHub repository to retrieve a file named sys.cache, uses it to extract a curl command, and downloads a shell script that fetches and stages CrashReporter.dmg in the /tmp directory.
  • After execution, CrashStealer establishes persistence as a LaunchAgent, validates the victim’s login password locally, unlocks the login keychain, and collects browser data, cryptocurrency wallet extensions, password manager data, keychain material, and files from Documents and Downloads.
  • The harvested data is packaged into a ZIP archive, encrypted with AES-GCM, and exfiltrated to an attacker-controlled server at 179.43.166[.]242.

VPN service favored by ransomware groups is sanctioned by US — Should Read

The U.S. sanctioned First VPN Service and its Ukrainian administrator for helping ransomware gangs hide their identities and infrastructure while attacking U.S. critical sectors. A Belarusian seller of malware-obfuscation tools was also sanctioned as part of a broader effort to disrupt cybercrime service providers.

  • The U.S. government sanctioned First VPN Service and its Ukrainian administrator, Dmytro Rashevskyi, for abetting ransomware gangs behind attacks on American municipalities, hospitals, schools, and businesses.
  • The Treasury Department said First VPN Service helped ransomware groups hide their identities, disguise malicious software, and evade detection, enabling attacks that caused billions of dollars in losses to U.S. critical infrastructure providers.
  • The Treasury Department said Rashevskyi used fake identities to buy infrastructure from companies that might otherwise refuse to do business with him due to abuse complaints tied to 1VPNS servers.
  • Belarusian national Yegeniy Vladimirovich Silayev was also designated for allegedly selling cryptors, which are methods used to make malware harder to detect by cloaking it as harmless files.
  • European law enforcement agencies and the FBI took down First VPN in May, saying the service had historically been used by cybercriminals to hide fraud, ransomware attacks, and other illegal activity.

Google and Microsoft Pull ModHeader With 1.6 Million Installs After Dormant Collector Found — Should Read

Google and Microsoft removed the popular ModHeader browser extension after researchers found a dormant browsing-history collection system hidden in the official Chrome and Edge versions. Although the collector’s allow-list was empty and no exfiltration was proven, it could have been activated through a routine update without new permissions.

  • Google and Microsoft removed the ModHeader browser extension from Chrome and Edge after researchers found a hidden browsing-history collector in the official store version.
  • Researchers said the collector was dormant because an internal allow-list shipped empty, and no proof has emerged that it ever collected or sent browsing domains.
  • The extension’s code could build a device fingerprint, encrypt visited domains, store up to 1,000 distinct domains locally, and post the data once a day to api.stanfordstudies.com if enabled.
  • The extension also pinged extensions-hub.com on install, update, and uninstall with the product, version, and browser.
  • Users are advised to remove ModHeader, ensure browser sync or managed policies do not reinstall it, and rotate any secrets such as API keys, bearer tokens, or session cookies that were pasted into it.

Lidl discloses online shop breach after service provider hack — Should Read

Lidl warned online shop customers in Germany, Belgium, and the Netherlands that attackers stole personal data from a separately stored file after hacking an IT service provider. The company says the shop system itself was not affected, but it cannot yet rule out exposure of passwords, addresses, bank details, or payment information.

  • Lidl notified customers in Germany, Belgium, and the Netherlands that attackers stole personal information in a breach at an IT service provider.
  • The breach involved a separately stored file containing online shop customer data, while Lidl said the online shop system itself was not affected.
  • The stolen data includes salutation, first and last name, telephone number, email address, date of birth, and customer number.
  • Lidl said it cannot yet rule out that affected customers' passwords, billing and delivery addresses, bank details, or other payment information may also be involved.
  • The hacked IT service provider filed a police report and engaged IT forensic experts, while Lidl notified the Dutch Data Protection Authority and warned customers about possible phishing attempts or identity fraud.

Attacker Uses Suspected AI-Generated PowerShell Script to Map Active Directory — Should Read

An attacker used pre-compromised RDP credentials and a likely AI-generated PowerShell script to aggressively enumerate Active Directory, stage files, and exfiltrate data. The incident highlights how AI is speeding up familiar intrusion playbooks rather than introducing fundamentally new techniques.

  • An unknown threat actor used pre-compromised credentials to gain RDP access to a domain-joined Windows Server and staged tools in the C:\ProgramData\ folder in early June 2026.
  • Huntress said the attacker used a likely AI-generated PowerShell script to locate the Domain Controller, enumerate Active Directory users, computers, groups, organizational units, and trusts, and create an AD_Report.html file.
  • The PowerShell script showed signs of AI assistance, including a prompt-like title, placeholder strings, over-engineered fallback methods, and beautified console output.
  • About 30 minutes after the Active Directory enumeration, the attacker deployed s5cmd and SharpShares to search for user-accessible data repositories before archiving and exfiltrating data to a remote server.
  • Sygnia reported a separate AI-assisted AWS cloud attack that progressed from initial access to broad compromise in about 72 hours using familiar cloud techniques rather than novel malware or zero-days.

Authenticated at Delivery, Forged at Origin — Should Read

A phishing email that failed SPF and DMARC at its origin was made to look legitimate after mailbox auto-forwarding gave it aligned authentication and ARC preserved the later pass verdict. The key takeaway is that defenders must inspect the full email hop chain and redirect path, not trust the final authentication result alone.

  • A fake eSignature notification failed SPF and DMARC at its origin hop but reached the reporting inbox with DKIM pass, DMARC pass, and compauth pass.
  • The message entered from 188[.]215[.]229[.]105, a Mailgun sending host recorded by Microsoft with spf=fail, dmarc=fail, and dkim=none at ingress.
  • A mailbox auto-forward gave the message a fresh aligned envelope sender, allowing SPF to pass on the new path while ARC preserved subsequent authentication results.
  • The call-to-action link used a Google open redirect, a nested ad-click redirect on adservice[.]google[.]com[.]ar, and ultimately led to ruslanstudio[.]com, a domain registered in 2022 to a registrant in Lalitpur, Nepal.
  • IRONSCALES Themis scored the message at 87% confidence and the platform auto-resolved it by moving it to junk roughly seven seconds after delivery.

Japan's largest taxi operator shuts systems after cyberattack — Should Read

Japan’s largest taxi operator, Nihon Kotsu, shut down parts of its systems after a malware-related cyberattack disrupted dispatch, reservations, web booking, and other services. The company is investigating whether data was leaked and has advised customers to watch for suspicious messages impersonating it.

  • Japan’s largest taxi and chauffeur operator by group revenue, Nihon Kotsu, said its internal systems were compromised by unauthorized external access involving a malware infection.
  • The incident occurred early Saturday morning and led the company to disconnect systems to prevent further damage.
  • Nihon Kotsu said car hire, web booking, reservation management, telephone dispatch, and some internal systems remain unavailable.
  • The company said its labor taxi service for pregnant women close to giving birth is suspended in Tokyo, Musashino City, Mitaka City, Tachikawa, Yokohama, and Saitama.
  • Nihon Kotsu has engaged external cybersecurity experts, is investigating whether data was leaked, and said no ransomware or extortion group had claimed responsibility at the time of writing.

UK charges suspects linked to Russian Coms call spoofing platform — Should Read

UK authorities charged five London suspects linked to Russian Coms, a caller ID spoofing platform used by criminals to make millions of scam calls by impersonating banks, telecoms firms, and law enforcement. The platform, shut down by the NCA, has been tied to roughly 170,000 victims and tens of millions in losses since 2020.

  • UK authorities charged five people from London following a National Crime Agency investigation into Russian Coms, a caller ID spoofing platform used by criminals to make over 1.8 million scam calls.
  • The charges include conspiracy to supply articles for use in connection with fraud, transferring or converting criminal property, and, for Zakkaria Sehailia, failing to comply with a notice to provide phone passcodes.
  • Russian Coms let criminals hide their identity by making calls appear to come from pre-selected numbers belonging to financial institutions, telecommunications companies, and law enforcement agencies.
  • Since 2020, Russian Coms has been linked to tens of millions in financial losses affecting an estimated 170,000 victims.
  • The NCA said criminals paid £1,200 to £1,400 in cryptocurrency for six-month contracts to use Russian Coms services before the platform was shut down.

When Mythos Owns The Loop: Self-Verifying Vulnerability Research — Should Read

Netskope used Anthropic’s Claude Mythos in self-verifying vulnerability research workflows against its own products, where separate model instances had to reproduce crashes or validate fixes before findings counted. The key takeaway is that frontier AI can now independently drive much of the vulnerability research loop, producing reproducible kernel, open-source, and binary-diff findings when grounded in strong verification harnesses.

  • Netskope used Anthropic’s Claude Mythos preview to run self-verifying vulnerability research against software that Netskope builds and ships.
  • Across three tracks, the model produced 9 kernel memory corruption findings behind a strict reachability bar, 17 previously unreported bugs in open source code used by Netskope products, and four confirmed n-day fixes reconstructed from a binary diff.
  • For kernel driver testing, a finding only counted when the model satisfied every runtime precondition between the entry point and unsafe sink and reproduced the crash three times from a clean snapshot.
  • For open source testing, findings had to be confirmed by a separate copy of Mythos in a clean sandbox against current upstream code using AddressSanitizer crashes.
  • For binary-diff testing, a patch-diff finding counted only if the same reproducer crashed the older build and ran cleanly on the latest build.

Russian celebrity journalist Ksenia Sobchak says hackers accessed Telegram channels via email breach — May Read

Russian journalist Ksenia Sobchak said hackers briefly hijacked her Telegram channels via an email breach and posted fabricated private correspondence. The Black Mirror group claimed it stole more than 350GB of her data, but the authenticity of the leak has not been verified.

  • Hackers briefly took control of several Telegram channels belonging to Russian journalist and media executive Ksenia Sobchak last week.
  • Sobchak said the hackers gained access through her email account and claimed the published screenshots of her interactions were fake.
  • The leaked materials carried the watermark of the hacker group Black Mirror, which claimed to have stolen more than 350 gigabytes of Sobchak's data spanning 2015 to 2026.
  • Black Mirror claimed Sobchak's archive includes conversations between her and senior Russian officials, as well as Andriy Yermak, the former head of Ukraine's presidential office.
  • The authenticity of the leaked material and the hackers' claims could not be independently verified.

Meta Files Patent for AI That Can Listen All Day and Track How You're Feeling — May Read

Meta filed a patent for an AI system that could continuously analyze a person’s voice, biometrics, eye signals, location, and device activity to infer and log their emotions over time. The system is not a current product, but it raises major privacy and regulatory concerns around always-on emotional profiling.

  • Meta filed patent application US 2026/0182881 for an AI system that can analyze a user’s speech throughout the day to infer emotional state and keep timestamped logs tied to context such as time, location, activity, and phone use.
  • The filing describes possible devices including smart glasses, phones, smartwatches, headphones, and smart home speakers, and says the system could use speech content, tone, pace, sighs, laughs, biometric signals, eye-tracking signals, and device-use behavior.
  • The patent application has not shipped in any Meta product, and Meta has not announced a product based on it.
  • The filing also describes a real-time fitness coach that could use smart glasses to watch workout form, respond to the user’s mood, ease off if the user seems tired or discouraged, or admonish the user if it decides they have energy and are slacking.
  • The article compares Meta’s filing to Amazon’s discontinued Halo Tone feature and notes that the EU AI Act bans AI emotion inference in workplaces and schools except for medical or safety reasons.

EU leaders eye social media ban for children under age 13 — Optional

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is considering an EU-wide minimum age of 13 for unsupervised social media use, citing concerns over children’s mental health and online safety. Several EU countries are already pursuing stricter rules, and platforms may be required to prove their services are safe and age-appropriate for teenagers.

  • European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she is considering a harmonized EU-wide delay to social media for children under age 13 who are not under the supervision of a caregiver.
  • Von der Leyen said children could receive gradual access once they turn 13, depending on proof from platforms that their services are age-appropriate and safe for teenagers.
  • Several EU countries, including France, Spain and Greece, have already imposed their own bans or are working with their legislatures to do so quickly.
  • Von der Leyen said European children spend an average of four to six hours a day watching a screen.
  • Most social media platforms already require users to be over age 12, but the article says those restrictions have been easily sidestepped without force of law.

Identity Due Diligence: The Missing Piece of M&A Risk Assessment — Optional

M&A cybersecurity due diligence often misses inherited identity risks such as exposed executive accounts, privileged users, contractors, and third-party credentials. Assessing identity exposure before closing can reduce integration risk, remediation costs, and post-acquisition security surprises.

  • Traditional M&A cybersecurity due diligence often focuses on technical controls such as vulnerability scans, network architecture, endpoint protection, security policies, and compliance certifications.
  • The article argues that acquisitions also transfer identity-related risk through employees, executives, contractors, vendors, privileged accounts, and other digital identities.
  • Identity exposure in a target organization may include exposed employee credentials, dormant privileged accounts, contractors with excessive access, targeted executive identities, and third-party vendors connected to critical systems.
  • Missing identity risk before an acquisition can increase integration risk, cause operational disruption, expand the attack surface, create regulatory and compliance challenges, and raise post-closing costs.
  • Identity Intelligence can help organizations assess exposure across employees, executives, contractors, and third parties and prioritize remediation after an acquisition.

What is a dependency firewall? — Optional

A dependency firewall blocks malicious open-source packages at install time, before they can run postinstall scripts or reach developer machines, CI, or AI coding agents. The article argues this is now necessary because supply-chain attacks move too quickly for after-the-fact scans or advisories to stop them.

  • A dependency firewall blocks malicious packages before they install, whether the install was requested by a developer, CI pipeline, or AI coding agent.
  • The article says install-time protection is needed because packages can execute code during installation, including through npm postinstall hooks that run with the developer's permissions.
  • The article cites the axios incident in which attackers hijacked a maintainer's npm account and added the malicious transitive dependency plain-crypto-js, whose postinstall hook dropped a cross-platform RAT.
  • The article says coding agents and MCP servers create new install surfaces because they can pull packages from npm on developer machines that have access to sensitive code and credentials.
  • A dependency firewall should check transitive dependencies for known malware, minimum package age, dependency confusion, typosquats, install script behavior, account takeover signals, and obfuscation techniques.

Introducing Precursor: detecting agentic behavior with continuous client-side signals — Optional

Cloudflare launched Precursor, a client-side session-based bot detection system that continuously analyzes behavioral signals like mouse movement, keyboard timing, focus, and visibility across a user journey. The goal is to better distinguish humans from automated or agentic traffic with fewer challenges for legitimate users.

  • Cloudflare launched Precursor, a client-side, session-based verification system that uses dynamically injected JavaScript to continuously collect behavioral signals as visitors interact with an application.
  • Precursor collects interaction signals such as pointer movement, keyboard activity, focus changes, and visibility, then sends buffered data to an edge evaluation layer for analysis.
  • The system is session-scoped, so behavioral data accumulates throughout a session and can contribute to Cloudflare bot score, challenge decisions, security rules, and detection improvement.
  • Cloudflare says Precursor is designed with privacy in mind by capturing keyboard timing and rhythm rather than actual keys pressed and by evaluating aggregate behavioral patterns internally.
  • Precursor is rolling out through the Cloudflare dashboard, is free until general availability later this year, and requires no application changes once enabled.

Rust-proof your code with our new Testing Handbook chapter — Optional

Trail of Bits added a new Rust chapter to its Testing Handbook covering security testing tools, review gotchas, memory zeroization, dependency vetting, and specialized testing like Miri, Clippy, proptest, and Kani. It also released rust-review, a Claude Code plugin for automated Rust security reviews.

  • Trail of Bits added a new chapter to its Testing Handbook that provides a comprehensive guide to security testing Rust programs.
  • The chapter covers Rust security guarantees and limitations, including unwind safety, nondeterminism, and arithmetic errors.
  • The chapter describes dynamic and static analysis tools and techniques, including Miri, proptest, coverage measurement, mutation testing, and Clippy.
  • The chapter includes guidance for manual Rust code reviews, including gotchas and footguns, operator precedence issues, and memory zeroization approaches.
  • Trail of Bits released rust-review, a Claude Code plugin co-built with Aptos Labs for automated Rust security reviews across more than a dozen bug classes.

Why cloud security is mission-critical for federal civilian and defense agencies — Optional

Tenable argues that cloud security is now a mission-critical requirement for U.S. federal civilian and defense agencies, especially for zero trust, continuous authorization, and protecting sensitive data. The article promotes Tenable One Cloud Exposure’s FedRAMP High and IL5 authorizations as a way to provide unified, compliant visibility and risk reduction across federal cloud environments.

  • The article states that cloud security is a mission imperative for federal civilian and defense agencies because cloud risks can affect citizen data, public services, mission readiness, national defense, and warfighter safety.
  • The article says federal cloud environments have become more complex due to multi-cloud architectures, containerized workloads, DevSecOps pipelines, and AI-powered applications.
  • The article argues that mature zero trust execution requires deep, real-time visibility across users, devices, applications and workloads, data, network and environment, automation and orchestration, and visibility and analytics.
  • The article states that FedRAMP High authorization and Impact Level 5 designation provide validation for protecting sensitive unclassified civilian data and supporting Department of War workloads.
  • The article says Tenable One Cloud Exposure has achieved FedRAMP High and IL5 authorization and is positioned as a unified platform for cloud risk reduction in federal cloud environments.

Thinking Fast and Slow in the SOC: The Case for Combining Autonomous AI with Analyst Copilots — Optional

The article argues that effective SOC AI should split work between an autonomous “fast brain” that investigates nearly all alerts at scale and analyst copilots for the small percentage of complex cases needing human judgment. Relying only on humans or general-purpose AI agents for raw alert triage leaves threats missed and analysts overloaded.

  • The article argues that most security teams are designing AI architectures that apply slow, deliberate analysis to work that should be handled automatically at scale.
  • Research cited in the article says 98% of alerts can be resolved autonomously, while less than 2% warrant human review.
  • The author says autonomous SOC systems should investigate all alerts continuously, correlate evidence across sources, close clear noise, and surface only the cases that need human attention.
  • The article positions tools such as Claude, Codex, and Cursor as best suited for complex case analysis, detection rule engineering, incident reporting, and threat hunting after an autonomous system has assembled the evidence.
  • The article argues that enterprises outsourcing alert investigation to MDR providers do not own the accumulated knowledge layer needed to make analyst copilots useful.

13th July – Threat Intelligence Report — Optional

Check Point’s 13 July threat intelligence roundup highlights major breaches, AI-driven attack risks, and critical vulnerabilities affecting routers, Linux KVM, U-Boot, and Opera GX. The key takeaway is that attackers are increasingly combining credential theft, supply-chain compromise, unpatched systems, and autonomous AI tooling to expand impact across organizations and infrastructure.

  • U.S. auto insurer AssuranceAmerica disclosed a data breach affecting approximately 7 million people after attackers used compromised employee credentials to access company systems and steal personal, insurance, vehicle, and claims information.
  • Latvia’s state-owned forestry company Latvijas Valsts Meži suffered a ransomware attack that disrupted multiple systems after attackers exploited a system that had remained unpatched for two years and leaked about 44GB of internal data.
  • Injective Labs experienced a supply chain compromise after attackers accessed its SDK project and published malicious npm packages that exfiltrated cryptocurrency wallet private keys and seed phrases.
  • Researchers profiled JadePuffer, an autonomous ransomware operation that used a large language model to exploit CVE-2025-3248 in an exposed Langflow instance, access a MySQL server, exfiltrate information, delete the database, and issue an extortion demand.
  • Several significant vulnerabilities were addressed or disclosed, including a Tenda router authentication backdoor, a critical Linux KVM flaw, U-Boot secure boot signature verification flaws, and an Opera GX browser issue that allowed malicious websites to install browser modifications without user confirmation.

Breach at the Beach: Play the Ultimate Entra ID CTF — Optional

Varonis is promoting Breach at the Beach, a free Entra ID capture-the-flag training experience designed to teach defenders how real-world identity and AI-related data exfiltration attacks can unfold. Players can complete online stages for CPE credits and themed badges, with in-person opportunities planned for Black Hat USA 2026 and DEF CON 34.

  • Varonis Threat Labs researchers Doron Kapah and Mark Vaitsman created Breach at the Beach, a free online Entra ID capture-the-flag training experience based on real cases they have encountered in customer environments.
  • The CTF follows Varonis’ threat-detecting cat Pixel as players trace an attacker’s steps in Entra ID to determine what sensitive data the attacker is trying to access.
  • The article says Entra ID is a control plane for users, applications, permissions, automation, and AI-powered workflows, and that non-human identities such as AI agents and service principals are expanding the attack surface.
  • Breach at the Beach is designed to teach players how legitimate features can be abused, how to work through raw Entra logs, and how to build defensive understanding without relying on large language models to solve challenges.
  • Completing each stage awards 1 CPE credit and a themed badge, and players who complete all four stages receive a certificate of completion to share on LinkedIn.

How to maintain code quality standards with AI code and vibe coding — Optional

AI-generated code can quickly create technical debt if teams skip consistent review, so code quality checks need to be scoped, rule-based, and integrated into both pull requests and repository scans. The article promotes Aikido’s Code Quality system as a way to provide faster, more consistent feedback than generic LLM reviews.

  • AI development tools are enabling developers and non-developers to ship applications and features faster, including changes inside larger existing applications.
  • The article warns that rapid AI-generated code without sufficient oversight can create technical debt, spaghetti code, strange bugs, and slower development over time.
  • The article says generic LLM code reviews lack the specific context and standards of a codebase, making them less reliable for maintaining code quality.
  • Aikido’s Code Quality feature runs LLM checks on a per-rule basis for pull requests and repository scans, with rules that can be fine-tuned or customized to match a team’s code style.
  • The article states that Aikido benchmarks and tunes prompts using manually labeled code samples, aiming to avoid flagging grey-zone issues that may frustrate developers.

OpenAI temporarily relaxes GPT-5.6 Sol usage limits — Optional

OpenAI temporarily removed the five-hour GPT-5.6 Sol usage limit for Plus, Pro, and Business users and reset current usage after heavy demand from Codex and ChatGPT Work. The company says efficiency improvements should make the model consume less usage going forward, though it is not necessarily unlimited.

  • OpenAI is temporarily removing the five-hour usage limit restriction for Plus, Pro, and Business plans after demand for GPT-5.6 Sol surged over the past 48 hours.
  • OpenAI also issued a one-time usage reset for everyone, giving users more room to use GPT-5.6 Sol for coding and agentic work.
  • Codex and ChatGPT Work count local messages and cloud-based tasks against a shared usage limit.
  • OpenAI product lead Tibo said the company is rolling out changes to make GPT-5.6 Sol more efficient across the board, which should result in less usage being consumed.
  • The temporary removal of the five-hour restriction does not necessarily make GPT-5.6 Sol completely unlimited.
